processing: Coarse, mature branches and leaves are cut, then either fixed and dried directly or, for the better southern-route zuo zhuang, fixed, steamed, rolled, pile-fermented and dried. The raw tea is pressed into Kang brick, Jin Jian, Fu brick or Fang Bao.
harvest_season: Mature leaf and current-year shoots, hand-picked or cut once grown; western-route tea uses even older material from branches of one to two years. Not a tea prized for early picking.
appearance_dry: Bricks or basket-packed tea with coarse leaf and stems, liver-brown in zuo zhuang, duller yellow-brown in the western teas.
appearance_liquor: Yellow-red and bright in southern-route tea, red-yellow in Fang Bao, red and clear in Fu brick.
appearance_wet: Coarse brown leaf, often with plenty of stem.
taste_profile: Plain and mellow with an aged-tea scent; Fang Bao carries a slight smoky note. Made to be boiled and drunk with butter or milk more than to be savoured on its own.

brewing.notes: Best simmered in a pot rather than steeped; several minutes suit coarse leaf and stems. Traditional use is with butter or milk.

vintage_note: Sold pressed, as Kang brick and Jin Jian from the southern route and Fu brick and Fang Bao from the western, with a production year on the wrapper. Southern tea has two broad classes and several grades. Ageing is valued but not formally tiered, so buy by type, grade and factory.
description:
Sichuan Bian Cha, border tea, is the old dark tea of Sichuan made for Tibetan and other western markets. It is a group, not one tea: southern-route tea from around Ya'an, today often called Tibetan tea, and the coarser western-route tea from around Dujiangyan, then called Guan County.

The material is deliberately rough: mature leaf and sometimes stems. Southern tea comes as mao zhuang, fixed and simply dried, or zuo zhuang, steamed and piled for a darker result. Western raw tea is fixed and sun-dried. Stems make up about 20% of raw tea for Fu brick and about 60% for Fang Bao.

In the cup it is mellow and warm, not complex. Southern tea is yellow-red and bright, western Fu brick red, with its golden flowers. Steeping it gongfu style misses the point; simmer it and try it with butter or milk.

When buying, name the type: Kang brick is finer than Jin Jian. Look for clean, aged smells, and do not worry about stems, which are normal here. Claims about slimming and longevity are best ignored.
history:
Tea from the Ya'an area was being sent toward Tibet in the Tang and Song, the root of the southern-route trade, and tea was exchanged for war horses at government-run tea-and-horse offices. Song offices are recorded at Ya'an, Yingjing, Tianquan and Hanyuan. The tea has been known by different names: Xi Fan tea in the Yuan, Wu Cha in the Ming and Tibetan tea today.

In the Qianlong period, the split was fixed: tea from Ya'an, Tianquan and Yingjing went to Kham and Tibet as southern-route tea, and tea from Guan County, Chongqing County and Dayi went to the Songpan area in the northwest as western-route tea. After 1949 production was mechanised under a policy of guaranteeing supply to border regions.
